opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, it really felt like we were standing at the very beginning of something, maybe five or six years ago, when "embodied intelligence" was not yet a phrase people in China used much. Cewu and I were both working on problems that sat between computer vision, 3D understanding, and robotics. We shared a strong feeling that the next big step for AI was not only about understanding images or text, but about agents that act in the physical world: grasping, manipulating, interacting with objects and people.

At that time, robotics and AI were still fairly separate communities. Vision people cared about benchmarks and datasets; robotics people cared about control, hardware, and reliability. Part of what we tried to do was build a bridge, bringing a data-driven, learning-centric mindset into robotics, and bringing physical grounding back into AI research. We organized talks, workshops, and discussions, and encouraged students to work on problems like generalizable grasping and articulated object manipulation, which seemed niche then.

Honestly, at first it was a bit lonely. People asked: is this real, or just a buzzword? Robots were expensive, data was scarce, and results were not as flashy as large models. But we believed the core bottleneck was clear: how do you get enough data, and the right representations, for a robot to generalize? That question pushed many of us toward simulation, synthetic data, and sim-to-real, which later became central to the whole field.

Now, when I see how hot embodied intelligence has become, with startups, capital, and young talent pouring in, I feel two things. One is gratitude. Those early efforts helped build a community and a shared language, and many of the students from that period are now leading the field. The other is a sense of responsibility. Hype can run ahead of reality. The hard problems are still hard: robust generalization, safety, cost, real deployment. So looking back, I'm proud we planted seeds early, but I also feel the real work is still ahead of us.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I think the honest word for it is "lonely." Around 2021, 2022, when Cewu and I started going around talking about embodied intelligence, most people in China's AI community hadn't even heard the phrase. We'd give a talk and people would ask, is this just robotics with a new name? And we'd have to explain: no, the point is that intelligence has to come from interacting with the physical world, from a body, from perception and action closed in a loop. Large language models were just starting to take off, and everyone's attention was there. Vision, language, that's where the money and the papers were. Robots were seen as slow, expensive, and a bit old-fashioned.

Cewu and I come at it from slightly different angles. He's deeper on the manipulation and the human-object interaction side, I came more from 3D vision and simulation, and I think that was actually a good combination. We could say, look, the perception problem and the action problem are the same problem, you can't separate them. We organized workshops, we pushed for it in the academic venues in China, we talked to funding agencies, we talked to a lot of students who were deciding what to work on. A big part of the early effort was just convincing good students that this was worth betting their PhD on, because at the time it looked risky.

What I'm proud of is that we didn't wait for the trend to arrive from the US and then follow it. We tried to build the community first, data, benchmarks, simulation tools, so that when the moment came, there would be people ready. And the moment did come, faster than I expected. Once large models showed that scaling works, people naturally asked, what about the physical world? Suddenly embodied intelligence was everywhere, every conference, every investor meeting.

If I'm honest, there's also a little bit of mixed feeling. When something becomes hot, a lot of noise comes with it, and some of the careful thinking we were trying to do gets drowned out. But I'd rather have that problem than the earlier one. The early period taught me that the hard part of promoting a direction isn't the technology, it's patience, and finding a few people who believe in the same thing and are willing to keep going when nobody is listening.

r001.rationale: He Wang describes the early effort as “lonely,” says most of China’s AI community had not heard of embodied intelligence, and recalls having to convince students it was worth pursuing—communicating the lack of a wider domestic scholarly coalition.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I think the most important part of those early efforts was helping people see embodied intelligence as a research direction worth taking seriously. The idea raises a fundamental question: how does intelligence develop through interaction with the physical world?

Working with Professor Lu Cewu, the challenge was to make that question concrete. It’s one thing to describe an intelligent robot; it’s another to build a system that can perceive, act, and adapt when things don’t go as expected. That gap gives researchers a lot to work on.

I wouldn’t frame it as something we alone promoted. A field grows through the efforts of many researchers and students. What matters to me is whether those early conversations encouraged people to tackle the hard problems—and whether we keep that focus as interest in embodied intelligence grows.

r001.rationale: The response says the field grew through many researchers and students, but does not state that their early advocacy lacked a wider domestic scholarly coalition.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think the important thing was helping people see embodied intelligence as a research direction worth taking seriously. Intelligence has to connect perception, decision-making, and action in the physical world, where conditions are uncertain and mistakes have consequences.

Working with Professor Lu Cewu, the challenge was how to make that vision concrete: what problems should we work on, and how would we know we were making progress? Promoting a direction is only the beginning. Ultimately, it needs to be supported by solid research and systems that work beyond a carefully controlled demonstration. That’s the perspective I would bring to those early efforts.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making embodied intelligence a serious research direction, but does not say their advocacy lacked a wider domestic scholarly coalition.
